TRAIN = TPAGN

∴ সঠিক উত্তর: ক) TPAGN

মানসিক দক্ষতা.question:
১০৬) যদি P অর্থ +, Q অর্থ ÷, R অর্থ × এবং S অর্থ - হয়, তাহলে নিচের রাশিটির মান কত?
64 Q 8 R 5 P 7 S 6 = ?
মানসিক দক্ষতা.exp:
প্রশ্ন: যদি P অর্থ +, Q অর্থ ÷, R অর্থ × এবং S অর্থ - হয়, তাহলে নিচের রাশিটির মান কত?
64 Q 8 R 5 P 7 S 6 = ?

সমাধান:
প্রদত্ত সাংকেতিক চিহ্নগুলো বসিয়ে পাই,
64 Q 8 R 5 P 7 S 6
= 64 ÷ 8 × 5 + 7 - 6

BODMAS-এর নিয়ম অনুযায়ী,
= 8 × 5 + 7 - 6
= 40 + 7 - 6
= 47 - 6
= 41

অতএব, রাশিটির মান = 41।

সঠিক উত্তর: গ) 41

মানসিক দক্ষতা.question: ১০৫) রিদওয়ান বলল, “মাহিরের মা আমার বাবার একমাত্র বোন।” মাহির, রিদওয়ানের সাথে সম্পর্ক কী?
মানসিক দক্ষতা.exp:
প্রশ্ন: রিদওয়ান বলল, “মাহিরের মা আমার বাবার একমাত্র বোন।” মাহির, রিদওয়ানের সাথে সম্পর্ক কী?

সমাধান:
রিদওয়ানের বাবার একমাত্র বোন = রিদওয়ানের ফুফু
মাহিরের মা = রিদওয়ানের বাবার একমাত্র বোন
অর্থাৎ, মাহিরের মা = রিদওয়ানের ফুফু
মাহির = রিদওয়ানের ফুফুর ছেলে
অর্থাৎ, ফুফুর ছেলে হলো ফুফাতো ভাই।

সুতরাং,
মাহির হলো রিদওয়ানের ফুফাতো ভাই।

সঠিক উত্তর: গ) ফুফাতো ভাই

Anatomy.question: ৯৪) Which part of a growing long bone contains the epiphyseal growth plate?
Anatomy.exp:
The metaphysis is the region between the diaphysis and epiphysis and contains the epiphyseal growth plate during growth.

• Diaphysis → shaft
• Metaphysis → growth plate region
• Epiphysis → end of bone
• Periosteum → outer connective tissue covering of bone.

Anatomy.question: ৩) Which cranial nerve carries the majority of parasympathetic fibres to the body?
Anatomy.exp:
The vagus nerve (CN X) carries the major proportion of cranial parasympathetic outflow and supplies the thoracic and most abdominal viscera.

Cranial parasympathetic outflow:
CN III → Edinger–Westphal nucleus → sphincter pupillae + ciliary muscle
CN VII → superior salivatory nucleus → lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands
CN IX → inferior salivatory nucleus → parotid gland
CN X → dorsal motor nucleus of vagus → heart, lungs and gastrointestinal tract up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon

Anatomy.question: ৬১) Which type of collagen is the principal collagen in basement membranes?
Anatomy.exp:
Type IV collagen forms the mesh-like network that provides structural support to basement membranes.

Collagen Types
Type I → bone, skin, tendon
Type II → cartilage, vitreous body
Type III → reticulin fibers, vessels
Type IV → basement membrane
Type VII → anchoring fibrils

Anatomy.question: ৫৩) Which cell is primarily responsible for the production of cerebrospinal fluid?
Anatomy.exp:
Choroid plexus epithelial cells, which are specialized modified ependymal cells, are primarily responsible for CSF production.

Choroid plexus → CSF production
Ependymal cells → line the ventricles and central canal
Astrocytes → support and maintain the blood–brain barrier
Oligodendrocytes → CNS myelination
Microglia → resident macrophages of the CNS.

Anatomy.question: ৭৭) Which component of the cytoskeleton is primarily responsible for forming the mitotic spindle?
Anatomy.exp:
The cytoskeleton consists of three major components:

• Microtubules → mitotic spindle, intracellular transport, cilia and flagella

• Microfilaments (actin) → cell movement, contraction and cytokinesis

• Intermediate filaments → mechanical strength and structural support

Anatomy.question: ৫১) The anterior pituitary is derived from:
Anatomy.exp:
Anterior pituitary → derived from Rathke’s pouch.
Rathke’s pouch → develops from surface ectoderm of the primitive oral cavity.
Posterior pituitary → derived from neuroectoderm of the diencephalon.
Neural crest → gives rise to structures including Schwann cells and adrenal medulla.

Anatomy.question: ৪৮) Which of the following is not a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
Anatomy.exp:
Podocytes are specialised cells of the visceral layer of Bowman’s capsule.
They form part of the glomerular filtration barrier, not the JGA.

Components of JGA
Macula densa
Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells
Extraglomerular mesangial cells

Functionsof JGA
Macula densa
Detects NaCl concentration in the distal tubule.
Participates in tubuloglomerular feedback.
Juxtaglomerular cells
Modified smooth-muscle cells of the afferent arteriole.
Secrete renin.
Extraglomerular mesangial cells
Located between the macula densa and renal arterioles.
Facilitate communication/signalling within the JGA.

Anatomy.question: ১৭৩) Which of the following is a holocrine gland?
Anatomy.exp:
In holocrine secretion, the entire secretory cell disintegrates and becomes part of the secretion.

• Holocrine → sebaceous gland
• Merocrine → eccrine sweat, salivary and pancreatic glands
• Apocrine → mammary and apocrine sweat glands

Anatomy.question: ১৮৬) Collection of neuronal cell bodies in the CNS is called:
Anatomy.exp:
A nucleus is a collection of neuronal cell bodies within the CNS.

CNS → nucleus = collection of neuronal cell bodies
PNS → ganglion = collection of neuronal cell bodies
CNS → tract = bundle of nerve fibres
PNS → nerve = bundle of nerve fibres.

Anatomy.question: ৮৩) What is the primary function of myoepithelial cells in exocrine glands?
Anatomy.exp:
Explanation
Myoepithelial cells are specialised contractile epithelial cells that surround glandular secretory units; their contraction compresses the secretory units and helps expel secretion into the ducts. Mucous cells secrete mucus, while absorptive epithelial cells perform absorption; basement membrane components are produced mainly by epithelial cells and connective-tissue cells.
 

Myoepithelial Cells: 
Specialised contractile epithelial cells associated with exocrine glands.
Location
Located between secretory epithelial cells and the basement membrane.
Surround the secretory units.
Function
Contract → compress secretory units → help expel glandular secretion into ducts.
Examples
Salivary glands
Lacrimal glands
Sweat glands
Mammary glands

Anatomy.question: ২৮) Which feature distinguishes the right lung from the left lung?
Anatomy.exp:
Explanation :

Right Lung
Has three lobes: superior, middle and inferior.
Has two fissures: oblique and horizontal.
Horizontal fissure separates the superior and middle lobes.

Left Lung
Has two lobes: superior and inferior.
Has an oblique fissure.
Cardiac notch and lingula are characteristic features.

Anatomy.question: ৫) Which cell in the liver is primarily responsible for storing vitamin A?
Anatomy.exp:
Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells are located in the space of Disse and store vitamin A. They also produce collagen during hepatic fibrosis.

• Kupffer cells → phagocytosis
• Hepatocytes → metabolism and bile production
• Cholangiocytes → line bile ducts

Physiology.question: ৯৯) Which sensory modality reaches the cerebral cortex without an initial relay through the thalamus?
Physiology.exp:
Olfaction is the classic exception because it initially reaches the cerebral cortex without a thalamic relay.

Thalamus

• Vision → relayed through the lateral geniculate nucleus.
• Hearing → relayed through the medial geniculate nucleus.
• Body sensation → relayed through the ventral posterior nuclei.
• Taste → relayed through the ventral posteromedial nucleus.
• Olfaction → initially bypasses the thalamus.
• Major functions → sensory relay, motor integration, arousal and consciousness.

Physiology.question: ৫০) Which of the following investigations best assesses the synthetic function of the liver?
Physiology.exp:
Explanation
• Prothrombin time is a sensitive, rapid marker of hepatic synthetic function because most clotting factors are synthesized by the liver and have relatively short half-lives.

Synthetic Functions of Liver
• Albumin synthesis
• Clotting factor synthesis
• Complement protein synthesis
• Transport protein synthesis
• Erythropoietin production
• Thrombopoietin production

Liver Function Tests:
• PT/INR, Albumin → Synthetic function
• ALT, AST → Hepatocellular injury
• ALP, GGT → Cholestasis
• Bilirubin → Excretory function

? PT/INR → most rapid indicator of impaired hepatic synthetic function.

Physiology.question: ১৭১) Which neurotransmitter is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS?
Physiology.exp:
GABA → major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

• Glutamate → major excitatory neurotransmitter
• GABA → major inhibitory neurotransmitter

Physiology.question: ৬৭) Which part of the adrenal gland produces glucocorticoids?
Physiology.exp:
• Zona fasciculata → glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol.

Adrenal gland
Adrenal cortex → GFR
• Zona glomerulosa → aldosterone
• Zona fasciculata → cortisol
• Zona reticularis → androgens

Adrenal medulla → catecholamines
• Adrenaline
• Noradrenaline

Physiology.question: ১৩৪) Which of the following cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
Physiology.exp:
• Total lung capacity includes residual volume.

• Residual volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry.
• Therefore, total lung capacity cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

Spirometry and lung volumes
Can be measured:
• Tidal volume
• Inspiratory reserve volume
• Expiratory reserve volume
• Vital capacity
• Inspiratory capacity

Cannot be measured:
• Residual volume
• Functional residual capacity
• Total lung capacity

** Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume.

Physiology.question: ১৫২) What is the renal clearance of glucose under normal conditions?
Physiology.exp: Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per unit time. Glucose clearance is normally zero because filtered glucose is completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

Physiology.question: ৮২) Which gut hormone is a major mediator of the incretin effect?
Physiology.exp:
GLP-1
 • Major incretin hormone released after meals.
 • Increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppresses glucagon secretion.
 • Its actions provide the physiological basis for important therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

Incretins
 • Main incretin hormones: GLP-1 and GIP.
 • Enhance insulin secretion after oral glucose.

DPP-4
 • Rapidly inactivates GLP-1 and GIP.
 • DPP-4 inhibitors prolong incretin action and are used in type 2 diabetes.

Incretin-based drugs
 • GLP-1 receptor agonists: Semaglutide, liraglutide.
 • DPP-4 inhibitors: Sitagliptin, linagliptin.
 • Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist: Tirzepatide.
 • Used in type 2 diabetes and obesity.

Physiology.question: ১২৬) Which organelle contains catalase?
Physiology.exp:
Peroxisomes contain catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂).

Lysosome
• Function → Intracellular digestion
• Enzymes → Acid hydrolases
• Breaks down → Cellular debris and damaged organelles

Peroxisome
• Function → Oxidation and detoxification
• Enzymes → Oxidases + catalase
• Catalase → Breaks down H₂O₂
• Key role → Very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation

Bio-chemistry.question: ১১২) Which vitamin is essential for collagen synthesis?
Bio-chemistry.exp:
• Vitamin C is essential for hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen synthesis.

• Deficiency → scurvy, with poor wound healing and bleeding gums.

? Vitamin C → collagen synthesis.

Bio-chemistry.question: ৬) Which part of the nephron is primarily responsible for glucose reabsorption?
Bio-chemistry.exp:
The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) reabsorbs virtually all filtered glucose under normal conditions, mainly via sodium–glucose cotransporters (SGLT).

Nephron Functions
• PCT → Glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na⁺ and water reabsorption
• Thick ascending limb → Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ reabsorption; water-impermeable
• DCT → NaCl reabsorption; calcium regulation
• Collecting duct → ADH-dependent water reabsorption

Bio-chemistry.question: ৩২) Which type of dietary fat is associated with the highest cardiovascular risk?
Bio-chemistry.exp:
Trans fat
  • Highest cardiovascular risk.
  • Increases LDL and decreases HDL.
  • Example: Processed foods containing partially hydrogenated oils.

 Saturated fat
  • Increases LDL cholesterol.
  • Cardiovascular risk is lower than trans fat.

 Monounsaturated fat
  • Generally has a favourable lipid effect.
  • Example: Olive oil.

 Polyunsaturated fat
  • Generally lowers LDL cholesterol.
  • Omega-3: Fatty fish.
  • Omega-6: Vegetable oils.


? Trans fat → highest cardiovascular risk.

Bio-chemistry.question: ৮৯) Which part of the gastrointestinal tract absorbs most nutrients?
Bio-chemistry.exp:
The jejunum is the major site of absorption of most nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract.

Major sites of absorption

• Duodenum → iron, calcium
• Jejunum → most nutrients
• Ileum → vitamin B₁₂ and bile salts
• Colon → water and electrolytes

? Jejunum → major site of nutrient absorption.

Bio-chemistry.question: ১০৮) Which of the following is not a basic step in protein production?
Bio-chemistry.exp:
• Replication duplicates DNA to maintain genetic information.
• It does not directly produce RNA or protein.

Sequential steps of protein production
1. Transcription
• DNA is used as a template to produce mRNA.
• RNA polymerase catalyses the formation of RNA from the DNA template.

2. Splicing
• Introns are removed and exons are joined.
• This produces mature mRNA for translation.

3. Translation
• Ribosomes read the mRNA sequence to synthesise a polypeptide.
• tRNA delivers the appropriate amino acids during protein synthesis.

4. Protein modification
• The newly synthesised polypeptide undergoes processing and folding.
• This produces the functional protein.

Pharmacology.question: ৪৭) Which drug exhibits zero-order elimination at therapeutic concentrations?
Pharmacology.exp:
Important examples

Zero-order → constant amount eliminated per unit time; 
• Example → Phenytoin, Ethanol, high-dose Aspirin

First-order → constant fraction eliminated per unit time.
•Example → most drugs

Pharmacology.question: ২৪) Which route of drug administration completely bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism?
Pharmacology.exp:
• Sublingual → directly absorbed through oral mucosa → completely bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism.

• Rectal → only partially bypasses first-pass metabolism.
• Oral/enteral → undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism.

Pharmacology.question: ১১৯) Which property of a drug determines the dose required to produce a specified effect?
Pharmacology.exp:
Potency
 • Determines the amount of drug required to produce a specified effect.
 • Greater potency means a lower dose is required.

Efficacy
 • Determines the maximum effect a drug can produce.

Pharmacology.question: ১৩) Which drug is the specific antidote for paracetamol poisoning?
Pharmacology.exp:
• N-acetylcysteine → It replenishes hepatic glutathione and enhances detoxification of the toxic metabolite NAPQI.

Common clinically used antidotes
• Paracetamol → N-acetylcysteine
• Opioids → Naloxone
• Benzodiazepines → Flumazenil
• Organophosphates → Atropine + pralidoxime
• Heparin → Protamine sulfate
• Warfarin → Vitamin K
• Iron → Deferoxamine

Pharmacology.question: ১৮০) Which drug has a narrow therapeutic index?
Pharmacology.exp:
• Digoxin → narrow therapeutic index → small difference between therapeutic and toxic concentrations.

Common drugs with narrow therapeutic index

• Digoxin
• Lithium
• Warfarin
• Phenytoin
• Theophylline

Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.question: ১৮) Which of the following are prerequisites for an autopsy?
Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.exp:
Proper lighting is an essential prerequisite for an autopsy. Consent from relatives is not required, and a magistrate’s order may be required, but the magistrate need not be physically present. Unrestricted public access is not a prerequisite.

Prerequisites of Autopsy:
Challan
Inquest report
Identification by police personnel not below the rank of SI
Authorized doctor
Ideal morgue with proper daylight/proper lighting

Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.question: ১০৭) Consent for a general physical examination of an outpatient is usually:
Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.exp:
1. Implied consent
 • Usually applies to routine general examination.
 • Patient’s voluntary presentation and cooperation imply consent.

2. Express consent
 • Consent is explicitly given by the patient.
  • Verbal consent → Minor procedures.
  • Written consent → Surgery and anaesthesia.

3. Informed written consent
 • Considered the gold standard for sensitive procedures.
 • Used for medico-legal examination of an alleged rape victim.

4. Blanket consent
 • General consent covering multiple examinations or procedures.
 • Does not replace specific informed consent when it is required.

Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.question: ১১৮) Which incision is most commonly used during a routine autopsy?
Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.exp:
I-shaped incision
 • Most commonly used routine autopsy incision.
 • Provides access to the thoracic and abdominal cavities.
 • Usually extends from the chin to the pubic symphysis, curving around the umbilicus.

Y-shaped incision
 • Used when detailed examination of the neck is required.
 • Particularly useful in suspected hanging or strangulation.

Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.question: ৮৪) Which finding is characteristic of a postmortem clot?
Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.exp:
Postmortem clot
 • Forms after death by passive coagulation of blood.
 • Has a smooth, shiny, gelatinous appearance.
 • Is not attached to the vessel wall and can be removed easily.
 • May form a red currant-jelly clot or yellow chicken-fat clot.

Antemortem thrombus
 • Forms during life and is firmly attached to the vessel wall.
 • Shows Lines of Zahn due to alternating layers of platelets/fibrin and red cells.

Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.question: ১১০) Which term describes a temporary period of apparent recovery between two periods of unconsciousness?
Forensic Medicine & Toxicology.exp:
Lucid interval is a temporary period of apparent normal consciousness or mental clarity. It is classically associated with extradural haemorrhage and may also occur in mental illness.
Forensic Terms:
Lucid interval → Temporary recovery of consciousness/mental clarity
Coup–contrecoup → Brain injury at the site of impact and/or opposite site
Suspended animation → Apparent cessation of vital functions
Death trance → State resembling death; may overlap with suspended animation

Community Medicine and Public Health.question: ৬৫) Which of the following is a major contraindication to combined OCPs?
Community Medicine and Public Health.exp:
• Classical migraine (migraine with aura) is a major contraindication to combined OCPs because of the increased risk of ischaemic stroke.

Major contraindications
 • Migraine with aura
 • Previous/current DVT or PE
 • Stroke or ischaemic heart disease
 • Severe hypertension
 • Current breast cancer
 • Severe liver disease/tumour
 • Heavy smoking at ≥35 years

Community Medicine and Public Health.question: ১১) Which type of vaccine is included for typhoid prevention in the Bangladesh EPI schedule?
Community Medicine and Public Health.exp:
Typhoid Vaccine

Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) contains Vi capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein. It provides a strong, durable immune response and is suitable for young children.

Vaccine Types & Examples

• Conjugate → TCV, PCV, Hib
• Live attenuated → BCG, MMR, OPV, rotavirus
• Recombinant subunit → Hepatitis B, HPV
• Inactivated → IPV, inactivated influenza
• Toxoid → Tetanus, diphtheria

Community Medicine and Public Health.question: ১৫১) In a community, the number of cases of a disease rises well above the expected level. What is this situation called?
Community Medicine and Public Health.exp:
Epidemic

The correct answer is epidemic because disease occurrence is above the expected level in a defined population, area, or period.

Epidemiological Terms

• Endemic → usual, persistent occurrence in a particular area/population.
• Epidemic → occurrence above the expected level.
• Sporadic → occasional, irregular occurrence.
• Pandemic → epidemic with widespread international spread.
• Outbreak → localized epidemic.

Community Medicine and Public Health.question: ১১৬) Which of the following is the most appropriate indicator of the nutritional status of preschool children?
Community Medicine and Public Health.exp:
Nutritional Assessment

• MUAC → Simple, rapid indicator of acute malnutrition in children
• BMI → More useful in older children and adults
• Serum albumin → Not a reliable routine indicator of nutritional status
• Haemoglobin → Assesses anaemia, not overall nutritional status

Community Medicine and Public Health.question: ১৮৯) Which of the following is the best measure for assessing the severity of an infectious disease?
Community Medicine and Public Health.exp:
Case Fatality Rate

• Measures → Severity / lethality among diagnosed cases
• Numerator → Deaths due to the disease
• Denominator → Diagnosed cases of the disease

Key Distinction

• Incidence → New cases
• Prevalence → Existing cases
• Mortality → Deaths in the population
• Case fatality → Deaths among cases

Pathology.question: ৮৮) Which is the hallmark of chronic inflammation?
Pathology.exp:
Tissue destruction is a characteristic feature of chronic inflammation, occurring along with persistent inflammation and attempts at healing.

Chronic Inflammation:

• Tissue destruction → Characteristic feature
• Mononuclear cells → Lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells
• Tissue repair → Angiogenesis and fibrosis
• Exudation → More characteristic of acute inflammation

Pathology.question: ১৪৭) Which is the most important factor in arterial thrombosis?
Pathology.exp:
• Endothelial injury is the key initiating factor in arterial thrombosis.

Virchow’s triad
 • Endothelial injury
 • Abnormal blood flow
 • Hypercoagulability

Pathology.question: ৮৫) Myocardial infarction is an example of:
Pathology.exp:
Myocardial infarction causes coagulative necrosis due to ischaemic injury, with preservation of the basic tissue architecture for some time.

Types of Necrosis:

• Coagulative → Myocardial infarction
• Liquefactive → Brain infarction; abscess
• Caseous → Tuberculosis
• Fat → Acute pancreatitis; traumatic fat necrosis

Pathology.question: ১৭৭) Which of the following is not an acute-phase protein?
Pathology.exp:
Acute-phase proteins are mainly synthesized by hepatocytes in response to inflammatory cytokines, especially IL-6. Interleukins are cytokines, not acute-phase proteins.

Acute-Phase Proteins:

• CRP
• Serum amyloid A
• Fibrinogen
• Haptoglobin
• Ferritin
• Ceruloplasmin
• Hepcidin

Pathology.question: ৪৪) Which complement component is the most potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils?
Pathology.exp:
C5a is a powerful chemotactic factor that attracts and activates neutrophils.
Complement – Important Functions
C3a → anaphylatoxin
C3b → opsonization
C5a → chemotaxis + neutrophil activation
C5b–9 → membrane attack complex
C3a and C5a → increase vascular permeability through mast-cell activation

Microbiology.question: ৫৪) What is the most common site of extrapulmonary tuberculosis?
Microbiology.exp:
• Lymph nodes → most common site of extrapulmonary TB.

Common extrapulmonary TB

• Lymph nodes → most common
• Pleura
• Bones and joints
• Meninges

Microbiology.question: ৭১) Which of the following is not a complication of measles?
Microbiology.exp: Bacterial pneumonia, otitis media, and diarrhoea are recognized complications of measles. Epididymo-orchitis is not a typical complication.

Microbiology.question: ১৩৯) Which of the following is an example of immune complex-mediated hypersensitivity?
Microbiology.exp:
Type I — Immediate, IgE-mediated
  • Anaphylaxis
  • Allergic rhinitis
  • Bronchial asthma
  • Urticaria

 Type II — Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity
  • Goodpasture syndrome
  • Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
  • Immune thrombocytopenia
  • Graves disease
  • Myasthenia gravis

 Type III — Immune complex-mediated
  • Serum sickness
  • SLE
  • Arthus reaction
  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

 Type IV — Delayed, T-cell-mediated
  • Contact dermatitis
  • Tuberculin reaction
  • Tuberculosis
  • Type 1 diabetes mellitus

Key point:
 • I → IgE | II → Antibody | III → Immune complex | IV → T cell

Microbiology.question: ৯৩) Löffler syndrome is classically associated with:
Microbiology.exp:
syndrome associations
  • Löffler syndrome → Ascaris lumbricoides
  • Löfgren syndrome → Sarcoidosis
  • Felty syndrome → Rheumatoid arthritis + splenomegaly + neutropenia
  • Dressler syndrome → Post-myocardial infarction autoimmune pericarditis
  • Reiter syndrome → Reactive arthritis

Microbiology.question: ১১৭) Which bacterial structure is not essential for survival?
Microbiology.exp: Plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA elements that are generally non-essential for bacterial survival, but may carry genes such as antimicrobial resistance.

Medicine.question: ১৭০) Which of the following is the most useful initial test for suspected hypothyroidism?
Medicine.exp:
Serum TSH is the most useful initial test for suspected primary hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism
Initial test → TSH
Primary hypothyroidism → ↑ TSH + ↓ free T4
Secondary hypothyroidism → ↓/inappropriately normal TSH + ↓ free T4
Common cause → Hashimoto thyroiditis

Medicine.question: ১৮৭) Which is the immediate treatment for severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?
Medicine.exp:
IV calcium gluconate is given immediately to stabilise the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. It does not lower serum potassium.
Hyperkalaemia — Immediate Management:
Calcium gluconate → Cardiac membrane stabilisation
Insulin + glucose → Rapid intracellular K⁺ shift
Salbutamol → Intracellular K⁺ shift
Dialysis → Definitive removal of K⁺ in severe/refractory cases

Medicine.question: ১৪২) Which of the following is an important clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome?
Medicine.exp:
Failure of lactation after childbirth is an important clinical feature of Sheehan syndrome, which results from postpartum pituitary insufficiency following severe postpartum haemorrhage.
Sheehan Syndrome
Cause → Severe postpartum haemorrhage
Failure of lactation → Prolactin deficiency
Secondary amenorrhoea → Gonadotrophin deficiency
Weakness/hypotension → Panhypopituitarism

Medicine.question: ৩৫) Which of the following snake bites is characteristically associated with neurotoxicity and minimal local swelling?
Medicine.exp:
Krait bite typically causes neurotoxicity with minimal or absent local swelling. Rapid Recall.pdf
Snake Bite — BCS Rapid Recall
Viper → Coagulopathy + bleeding + local swelling
Cobra/King cobra → Neurotoxicity + local swelling
Krait → Neurotoxicity + minimal local swelling
Sea snake → Neurotoxicity + myotoxicity/rhabdomyolysis
Neurotoxicity → Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness → respiratory paralysis

Medicine.question: ১৭৯) Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs is preferred for use during pregnancy?
Medicine.exp:
Insulin is the preferred anti-diabetic treatment during pregnancy when pharmacological treatment is required.
Diabetes in Pregnancy
Preferred treatment → Insulin
Insulin → Does not cross the placenta
Metformin → May be used in selected cases
Oral agents → Generally not preferred as first-line therapy in pregnancy

Medicine.question: ৯৫) Which of the following is not a component of pellagra?
Medicine.exp:
Pellagra is caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency and classically presents with the 3 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
Dermatitis → Photosensitive, symmetrical rash
Diarrhoea → Gastrointestinal manifestation
Dementia → Neuropsychiatric manifestation
Dysphagia → Not a classical component of pellagra

Medicine.question: ৬৩) Which of the following is the first-line management of conscious hypoglycaemia?
Medicine.exp:
Oral glucose is the first-line treatment for a conscious patient with hypoglycaemia.
Hypoglycaemia
Conscious → Oral glucose
Unconscious → IV dextrose
No IV access → IM glucagon
Recheck blood glucose → After treatment

Medicine.question: ১৩৬) Which anti-tuberculous drug is associated with peripheral neuropathy?
Medicine.exp:
Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy, which is prevented or treated with pyridoxine (vitamin B₆).
Anti-TB Drugs — Key Adverse Effects
Isoniazid → Peripheral neuropathy
Ethambutol → Optic neuritis
Rifampicin → Orange-red body fluids
Pyrazinamide → Hyperuricaemia
Isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide → Hepatotoxicity

Medicine.question: ১৫) Which drug is used to reduce proteinuria in diabetic nephropathy?
Medicine.exp:
Explanation


Diabetic Nephropathy :
ACE inhibitors (e.g., enalapril) reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria, providing renal protection in diabetes, particularly with hypertension or albuminuria

• ACE inhibitor → ↓ Proteinuria + renal protection
• ARB → Alternative when ACE inhibitor is not tolerated
• SGLT2 inhibitors → Also provide important renal protection in diabetic CKD

Medicine.question: ২১) Which of the following is a positive symptom of schizophrenia?
Medicine.exp:
Thought broadcasting is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia, in which the patient believes that their thoughts are accessible to others.

Schizophrenia — Clinical Features
First-rank/positive symptoms — ABCD
A → Auditory hallucinations
B → Broadcasting/insertion/withdrawal of thoughts
C → Controlled feelings, impulses or acts (passivity)
D → Delusional perception

Negative symptoms
Flattened/blunted affect
Apathy and avolition
Social withdrawal
Poverty of speech (alogia)
Poor self-care
Cognitive impairment
Impaired attention
Memory impairment
Executive dysfunction

Medicine.question: ৪৫) Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of multiple myeloma?
Medicine.exp:
Multiple Myeloma — Key Features

• Bone → Lytic lesions + bone pain
• Blood → Anaemia + monoclonal paraprotein
• Calcium → Hypercalcaemia
• Kidney → Renal impairment
• Marrow → Plasma-cell infiltration


Multiple myeloma → CRAB: HyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions.

Medicine.question: ৫৭) Which of the following is a component of the CURB-65 score?
Medicine.exp:
Respiratory rate ≥30/min is one of the five components of the CURB-65 score, which is used to assess the severity of community-acquired pneumonia.
CURB-65
C → Confusion
U → Urea >7 mmol/L
R → Respiratory rate ≥30/min
B → Blood pressure <90 mmHg systolic or ≤60 mmHg diastolic
65 → Age ≥65 years

Medicine.question: ২৬) Thunderclap headache is a characteristic feature of:
Medicine.exp:
Headache - Associations

• Subarachnoid haemorrhage → Thunderclap headache
• Migraine → Unilateral, pulsatile ± aura
• Tension-type → Bilateral, pressing/tightening
• Cluster → Unilateral orbital pain + autonomic features
• Meningitis → Headache + fever + neck stiffness
• Raised ICP → Morning headache + vomiting ± papilloedema

Medicine.question: ২০০) Which of the following is a characteristic sign of Stevens–Johnson syndrome?
Medicine.exp:
Nikolsky sign is characteristic of Stevens–Johnson syndrome, indicating epidermal separation with gentle lateral pressure.
Nikolsky sign → Stevens–Johnson syndrome, pemphigus
Koebner phenomenon → Psoriasis
Auspitz sign → Psoriasis
Darier sign → Urticaria pigmentosa (cutaneous mastocytosis)

Medicine.question: ১২৫) What is the first-line treatment for scabies?
Medicine.exp:
Scabies

• First-line treatment → Permethrin 5% cream
• Apply overnight from neck down and wash off after 8–14 hours.
• Treat close household/sexual contacts simultaneously.
• Oral ivermectin → Alternative, especially for outbreaks or difficult-to-treat cases.

Medicine.question: ৭৫) Which of the following is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis?
Medicine.exp:
Explanation
Graves’ disease is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis.
Thyrotoxicosis
Most common cause → Graves’ disease
Graves’ disease → Diffuse goitre + ophthalmopathy
Toxic multinodular goitre → More common in older people
Thyroiditis → Release of preformed thyroid hormones

Medicine.question: ১৭৫) Mycobacterium leprae shows a characteristic tropism for which cell?
Medicine.exp:
Leprosy — Cellular Tropism

M. leprae has a characteristic tropism for Schwann cells, resulting in peripheral nerve involvement and sensory loss.

• Target cell → Schwann cell
• Major consequence → Peripheral neuropathy
• Clinical feature → Loss of pain and temperature sensation

Surgery.question: ১৬) Which vitamin deficiency is most likely in obstructive jaundice?
Surgery.exp:
• Obstructive jaundice → ↓ Bile reaching intestine
• Result → ↓ Fat absorption
• Vitamin K deficiency → Prolonged PT/INR and bleeding tendency

Surgery.question: ১৬৪) Which type of shock is most commonly encountered in surgical practice?
Surgery.exp:
Hypovolaemic shock is common in surgical practice, mainly due to haemorrhage or severe fluid loss.

Types of Shock: 

• Hypovolaemic — “VOLUME LOSS”
• Haemorrhage, dehydration, burns

• Cardiogenic — “PUMP FAILURE”
• Acute myocardial infarction, severe heart failure

• Septic — “INFECTION + VASODILATATION”
• Severe infection → systemic vasodilatation

• Anaphylactic — “ALLERGIC”
• Severe hypersensitivity reaction → vasodilatation

• Neurogenic — “LOSS OF SYMPATHETIC TONE”
• Spinal cord injury → vasodilatation + bradycardia

• Obstructive — “MECHANICAL BLOCK”
• Pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax

Surgery.question: ১১৫) Which of the following is the most specific test for pancreatic exocrine function?
Surgery.exp: Faecal elastase is a useful non-invasive test for assessing pancreatic exocrine function.

Surgery.question: ১২) Which is the earliest symptom of acute intestinal obstruction?
Surgery.exp:
Colicky abdominal pain is usually the earliest symptom, caused by increased peristalsis against the obstruction.

Important Clinical Features of Intestinal Obstruction

• Earliest symptom: Colicky abdominal pain
• Small bowel / proximal obstruction: Early, prominent vomiting
• Large bowel / distal obstruction: Prominent constipation + abdominal distension
• Later: Absolute constipation / obstipation
• Sudden severe continuous pain: Strangulation / ischaemia

Surgery.question: ৪১) Which of the following conditions is treated by Heller myotomy?
Surgery.exp:
Heller myotomy is a surgical treatment for achalasia in which the lower oesophageal sphincter muscle is divided to relieve obstruction.

Important Operations
• Heller myotomy → Achalasia
• Ramstedt pyloromyotomy → Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
• Lichtenstein repair → Inguinal hernia
• Whipple procedure → Pancreatic head malignancy

Surgery.question: ৪০) What is the most commonly used method for inguinal hernia repair?
Surgery.exp: Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair is the commonly used open surgical technique for inguinal hernia repair.

Surgery.question: ১৯০) Which of the following is a main component of the secondary survey in ATLS?
Surgery.exp:
ATLS — Survey Sequence

• Primary survey → ABCDE
• A → Airway + cervical spine protection
• B → Breathing
• C → Circulation + haemorrhage control
• D → Disability
• E → Exposure + prevent hypothermia
• Resuscitation → Performed simultaneously with the primary survey; treat life-threatening problems immediately.
• Secondary survey →
• Detailed head-to-toe examination
• AMPLE history → Allergies, Medications, Past history/Pregnancy, Last meal, Events

Surgery.question: ১০১) Which type of burn is an indication for hospital admission?
Surgery.option1: 5% burn involving the trunk of an adult
Surgery.option2: 10% burn involving the trunk of a child
Surgery.option4: 10% circumferential burn of the lower limb
Surgery.exp: Inhalational burn is an important indication for hospitalisation because of the risk of airway injury and respiratory complications.

Surgery.question: ৯০) Avascular necrosis is most commonly associated with:
Surgery.exp:
Avascular Necrosis

• Most common site → Femoral head
• Important causes → Corticosteroid use, alcohol, trauma, sickle cell disease
• Early investigation → MRI is most sensitive.

Surgery.question: ৬৪) Which is the most common site of breast carcinoma?
Surgery.exp:
The upper outer quadrant is the most common site of carcinoma of the breast.

Breast Carcinoma 
• Commonest site → Upper outer quadrant
• Commonest histological type → Invasive ductal carcinoma
• Common lymphatic spread → Axillary lymph nodes
• Important warning sign → New breast lump in an adult woman

Surgery.question: ৭০) In triage, which colour category is assigned to a patient requiring urgent care?
Surgery.exp:
Triage Colour Coding
•  Red → Immediate priority
• Yellow → Urgent priority
• Green → Minor / non-urgent
•  Black → Dead / expectant

Surgery.question: ১১১) Which of the following is not used to assess the severity of acute pancreatitis?
Surgery.exp:
Important Severity Score
• Ranson criteria → Acute pancreatitis
• APACHE II → Acute pancreatitis and critically ill patients
• BISAP → Acute pancreatitis
• Glasgow-Imrie criteria → Acute pancreatitis
• Child–Pugh → Chronic liver disease/cirrhosis
• Wells score → thromboembolic risk

Surgery.question: ৭২) Which of the following is an example of distributive shock?
Surgery.exp:
Types of Shock
Distributive shock
• Septic shock
• Anaphylactic shock
• Neurogenic shock

Hypovolaemic shock
• Haemorrhage
• Burns
• Dehydration

Obstructive shock
• Air embolism
• Cardiac tamponade
• Tension pneumothorax

Cardiogenic shock
• Acute myocardial infarction
• Severe arrhythmia
• Cardiomyopathy

Surgery.question: ১৩৮) Which of the following is a contraindication to circumcision?
Surgery.exp:
Hypospadias is a contraindication to circumcision because the prepuce may be required for reconstructive urethral surgery.

Circumcision — Important Exam Points

• Indications
• True phimosis
• Paraphimosis
• Recurrent balanitis/balanoposthitis
• Recurrent UTI in selected cases
• Contraindications
• Hypospadias
• Epispadias
• Buried/concealed penis
• Chordee
• Important complication
• Bleeding → usually from the frenular artery or branches of the dorsal penile vessels.

Surgery.question: ১৬২) Which physical examination finding is characteristic of an inguinal hernia?
Surgery.option3: Inability to get above the swelling
Surgery.exp:
An inguinal hernia extends through the inguinal canal, so its upper limit cannot be reached on examination.

Inguinal Hernia :
• Cannot get above the swelling
• Usually reducible
• Cough impulse usually positive
• Transillumination negative
• May extend into the scrotum

Hydrocele: 
• Can get above the swelling
• Not reducible
• Cough impulse negative
• Transillumination positive
• Usually fluctuant

Surgery.question: ১৫৯) Rodent ulcer is a characteristic lesion of which disease?
Surgery.exp:
Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC)
• Rodent ulcer
• Site → Face, especially nose
• Pearly, rolled edge
• Locally destructive; rare metastasis

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
• Site → Sun-exposed skin
• Scaly, indurated lesion
• Ulceration may occur
• Metastasis → Possible

Malignant Melanoma
• Site → Skin, commonly trunk/lower limb
• ABCDE → (Asymmetry, Border, Colour, Diameter, Evolution)
• Pigmented lesion
• Early metastasis

Surgery.question: ১০৪) Which clinical feature is most characteristic of large bowel obstruction compared to small bowel obstruction?
Surgery.exp:
Large bowel obstruction typically causes early and prominent constipation/obstipation, whereas vomiting is usually a later feature.

Clinical Features

Large Bowel Obstruction
• Early prominent constipation → obstipation
• Marked abdominal distension
• Colicky abdominal pain
• Vomiting → usually late

Small Bowel Obstruction
• Vomiting → usually early and prominent
• Central abdominal distension
• Colicky abdominal pain
• Constipation/obstipation → particularly with complete obstruction

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৯৮) Which hormone is mainly responsible for constipation during pregnancy?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: • Progesterone relaxes intestinal smooth muscle and reduces gastrointestinal motility during pregnancy.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৬৬) When is the routine fetal anomaly scan typically performed?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: The routine fetal anomaly scan is performed at around 18–22 weeks to assess fetal anatomy and detect structural abnormalities.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ২৫) What is the most common cause of false labour pain?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular uterine contractions that may cause discomfort but do not produce progressive cervical dilatation.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ২) Which immunoglobulin is transferred across the placenta?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp:
IgG is the only major immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta, providing passive immunity to the fetus.

IgG1 → Most efficient placental transfer

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৯২) Which analgesic is generally preferred for fever or mild pain during pregnancy?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is generally preferred for mild pain or fever during pregnancy when used appropriately.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৯৭) Which is the most common complication of uterovaginal prolapse?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: A decubitus ulcer may develop on the exposed, chronically prolapsed cervix due to friction and pressure.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৬০) What is the characteristic clinical feature of amniotic fluid embolism?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: Cyanosis is a characteristic feature of amniotic fluid embolism due to acute respiratory compromise and hypoxaemia.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৭৪) What is the most common indication for induction of labour?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: Post-term pregnancy is a common indication for induction of labour to reduce the risks associated with prolonged pregnancy.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৫৮) Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp:
Losartan, an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can cause fetal renal injury, oligohydramnios, and fetal death.

Key Point:
• Pregnancy → Avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs
• Preferred → Labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৪) Which is the most common cause of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp:
• Chlamydia trachomatis → common cause of PID.
• N. gonorrhoeae → also an important cause.

? PID → Chlamydia trachomatis

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৩০) Which scoring system assesses cervical favourability before induction of labour?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: The Bishop score assesses cervical favourability before induction of labour and helps predict the likelihood of successful induction.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৩৮) Which is the most common fetal lie at term?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp:
• Longitudinal lie is the most common fetal lie at term.

More About Fetal Lie:

• Longitudinal lie → fetal long axis is parallel to the maternal long axis.
• Transverse lie → fetal long axis is perpendicular to the maternal long axis.
• Oblique lie → fetal long axis lies at an angle to the maternal long axis.
• Transverse/oblique lie → increases the risk of shoulder presentation and obstructed labour.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ৮০) What is the most common presenting feature of placental abruption?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: Painful vaginal bleeding is the classic presenting feature of placental abruption, often associated with uterine tenderness and increased uterine tone.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৭৮) What is the definitive treatment for eclampsia after the mother has been stabilised?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: • Delivery/termination of pregnancy is the definitive treatment for eclampsia after maternal stabilisation.

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১০৯) How many ANC contacts are recommended in the WHO ANC model?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp:
• WHO ANC model → 8 contacts during pregnancy.

? WHO ANC → 8 contacts

Obstetrics and Gynaecology.question: ১৩৫) Which is the most common presenting symptom of carcinoma of the cervix?
Obstetrics and Gynaecology.exp: • Postcoital bleeding is a classic presenting symptom of carcinoma of the cervix.
